elements.text: Electrical Properties and the Thermal and Photochemical Stability of Poly(vinyl chloride) Films Stabilized With Some Maleyl Amide Polymers
S.T. Rabie
Photochemistry Department, National Research Centre, Dokki, Cairo, Egypt
M.A.M. Eid
Microwave Physics Department, National Research Centre, Dokki, Cairo, Egypt

Some maleyl amide polymers were prepared and evaluated as thermal and photochemical stabilizers for rigid poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC). Thermal degradation was determined by measuring the rate of dehydrochlorination potentiometrically. Also, the degree of discoloration was measured for both the thermally degraded and the photochemically degraded PVC. Dibutyltin maleate heat stabilizer was used for comparison in thermal and photodegradation. The applied polymers showed stabilizing efficiency in both thermal and photodegradation by decreasing the rate of degradation, degree of discoloration, and percentage weight loss. The amide polymer of melamine gave better stabilizing efficiency than those of p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine. A dielectric study was carried out over a frequency range from <sup>100</sup> <sup>Hz</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>100</sup> <sup>kHz</sup> <sup>at</sup> <sup>room</sup> <sup>temperature</sup> <sup>(</sup>∼<sup>22</sup>8<sup>C).</sup> <sup>The</sup> results revealed that the stabilizing effect of these maleyl amide polymers depends on the type of stabilizer and its concentration. The dielectric data for the investigated systems were found to be fitted by two absorption regions using the Fro¨hlich function. These regions are ascribed to the Maxwell–Wagner effect and to intramolecular motion involving the rotation of various segments of the side group as the main chain motion is restricted. The study led to a conclusion that the greater stabilizing efficiency of the melamine amide polymer may be due to the presence of a free amino group (NH<sub>2</sub>) that can participate in the stabilization process. INTRODUCTION

Stabilization of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) against thermal as well as photodegradation is essential for processing and application of the polymer. These degradation processes result in a deterioration of mechanical and electrical properties. The most critical feature is the discoloration of PVC. This discoloration could be attributed to the conjugation of double bonds and a polyene structure [1– 3]. The PVC suffers poor thermal and light stability that may be due to an autocatalytic dehydrochlorination reaction initiated at the labile sites in the polymer chain [4].

In order to impart good light stability to PVC, a good thermal stabilizer may be introduced. This stabilizer could prevent the formation of CO groups and polyene sequences which are responsible for the absorption of UV light and, therefore, for light degradation. The thermal stabilizer is able to bind the hydrogen chloride formed during degradation, and so a certain light protection effect is achieved [5, 6].

Thermal dehydrochlorination of PVC begins with internal allylic chloride, and tertiary chloride structural defects formed during polymerization. Mechanisms for the formation of all the labile defects are well-established. During thermal degradation, ordinary monomer units are converted into internal allylic chloride defects by a mechanism that may include the abstraction of hydrogen by triplet cation diradicals derived from polyene intermediates [7]. Thermal degradation studies have been carried out in the presence of different metal carboxylates. It is found that the main role of metal soap stabilizers is the blocking of the fast-zip elimination of HCl from the PVC chain [8].

Various investigators have studied the effect of heat stabilizers as well as dibutyltin maleate (DBTM) and its effect on the photodegradation of PVC [9]. The effects of DBTM and dioctyltin thioglycolate on the photodegradation of PVC were compared. Cooray and Scott [10] found that both heat stabilizers have a stabilizing effect against the photodegradation of PVC. Braun et al. [11] synthesized and investigated some polymeric stabilizers as costabilizers for PVC. It was found that these polymers were capable of increasing the induction time of PVC dehydrochlorination. This costabilizing effect is dependent on the amount of functional groups which has been introduced into the copolymer. The new costabilizers interact with most kinds of stabilizers used and are capable of partly substituting for the metal stabilizers [11].

The AC electrical studies of polymers reveal some structural details and add valuable complementary information to the electrical application of polymer materials. One of the main advantages of frequency-dependent measurements is that the contributions of the bulk materials and the grain boundary effects can easily be represented [12, 13]. In addition, dielectric relaxation, which is due to a number of different polarization mechanisms, is observed under the AC field. Each relaxation process may be characterized by a relaxation time that describes the decay of its polarization with time in a periodic field.

The present work aims to examine the thermal and photochemical stability effects of the applied maleyl amide polymers as stabilizers for rigid PVC. The dielectric properties of the stabilized PVC were investigated. This was accomplished by measuring permittivities, loss factors, and the relaxation processes that may appear in virgin samples as well as in the treated ones in the investigated range of frequency.
EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Materials

Poly(vinyl chloride) (suspension grade) with $K = 6 7$$M _ { \mathrm { w } } = 1 4 0 { , } 4 0 0 ,$$M _ { \mathrm { n } } = 3 8 { , } 7 0 0 ,$and $M _ { \mathrm { w } } / M _ { \mathrm { n } } ~ = ~ 3 . 6$was obtained from the El-Ameria Company for Petrochemicals, Alexandria, Egypt. Tetrahydrofuran (THF) was obtained from Merck-Schuchardt, Mu¨nchen; dibutyltin maleate was supplied by Ciba-Geigy. The THF was distilled over potassium under $\mathrm { N } _ { 2 } .$. All solvents were distilled before use.
Preparation of Maleyl Amide Polymers
Polycondensates of maleic acid and m-phenylenediamine, p-phenylenediamine, or melamine were prepared by Abd-El-Ghaffar et al. [14].
Preparation of PVC Samples for Thermal and Photodegradation

The PVC samples were prepared for thermal degradation by thoroughly mixing 200 g of PVC with 2% by weight of the applied compounds. Evaluation of the thermal oxidative degradation of PVC in air was carried out by continuous potentiometric determination of the evolved HCl gas [15], which was plotted against time of degradation at $( 1 8 0 \pm 1 ) ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$, using a digital pH meter with an Ag electrode and a reference calomel electrode.

The PVC films were prepared for photodegradation by grinding the PVC thoroughly with each of the applied stabilizers at various concentrations (0.5, 1, and 2% by weight) in order to cast films of the blends from purified THF [16]. The solution was poured into a Petri dish of known diameter, and the film was obtained after solvent evaporation in a desiccator. The film was then washed with diethyl ether in order to remove the rest of the THF [17].

The PVC films prepared in the absence and in the presence of the applied materials were exposed to the light source (high-pressure $\mathrm { H g }$lamp, HPK 125 W). The distance between the samples and the light source was 20 cm, and the temperature was ${ \approx } 3 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$. The exposure time intervals were 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h. The degree of discoloration of the photodegraded samples was measured colorimetrically as a function of irradiation time, a Perkin-Elmer UV-visible spectrophotometer, Lambda 3, being used. Thermogravimetric analysis of the investigated amide polymers and photodegraded stabilized PVC samples was carried out by using a Perkin-Elmer TGA7 thermal analyzer.
Dielectric Measurements

The permittivity $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and dielectric loss $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$in the frequency range 100 Hz up to 100 kHz were measured by using an LCR meter, Type AG-411 B (Ando Electric, Japan). Two parallel glass plates were coated on one side with gold and used as a measuring cell. The cell was calibrated by using standard materials with different thicknesses ranging from 0.005 to 0.05 mm. For each sample a relation between the thickness d and its capacitance $C _ { \mathbf { M } }$was plotted as a standard curve. The capacitance $C _ { \mathbf { M } }$for the standard materials obtained from the standard curves was plotted versus the known permittivity $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$of each material. The relation between $C _ { \mathbf { M } }$and $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$was found to be linear; thus, the permittivity corresponding to any measured capacitance could be deduced. The capacitance $C _ { \mathbf { M } }$and the loss tangent tan d obtained directly from the LCR were used to calculate $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime } .$The experimental errors in $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$were found to be 63 and 65%, respectively. The temperature of the cell was controlled to within $\pm 0 . 1 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$by the circulation of water from an ultrathermostat through a jacket surrounding the cell.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Thermal Stabilization Study of PVC

Results of the dehydrochlorination of rigid PVC stabilized by the maleyl amide polymers during thermal degradation at $1 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$are shown in Fig. 1. Data on the nonstabilized blank sample and that stabilized by the industrial heat stabilizer DBTM are also given for comparison. In all experiments the stabilizers were used in a concentration of 2% by weight. The results show that maleyl amide polymers are more efficient than the industrial stabilizer (DBTM). The greater efficiency is indicated by the longer induction period $T _ { \mathrm { S } } ,$during which no detectable amounts of HCl evolved. As shown in Fig. 1, the $T _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$values for the amide polymers of melamine, p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine were found to be 40, 28, and 18 min, respectively, while the $T _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$of the PVC sample stabilized by the reference heat stabilizer DBTM was 13 min. Also, the rate of dehydrochlorination and hence that of the degradation process was lowered upon using the polymeric stabilizers.

Another proof for the stabilizing efficiency of the maleyl amide polymers is the extent of discoloration of the thermally degraded PVC. Figure 2 shows that the degraded PVC samples stabilized by the investigated compounds have lower degrees of discoloration than that stabilized by DBTM. From Figs. 1 and 2, it is clear that the melamine amide polymer has a greater stabilizing effect on PVC than the p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine polymers.

Qualitative elemental analysis of the thermally degraded PVC samples was performed after extensive washing with boiling water, ethanol, and then diethyl ether, followed by drying overnight at $4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$in order to remove any residual stabilizer. The elemental analysis showed the presence of nitrogen, thereby indicating the attachment of the stabilizer molecules to the polymeric chain.

The stabilization may be taking place through the abstraction of the amidic H-atom by the Cl<sup></sup> radical and the attachment of the stabilizer radical to the degraded PVC radical chain, thus disrupting the chain degradation and consequently the formation of conjugated double bonds, thereby leading to a lower degree of discoloration.
This mechanism may be confirmed by the IR spectrum of the PVC degraded in the presence of the stabilizer.

The absence of the stretching and bending bands of the NH amide group at $3 5 0 0 { - } 3 1 0 \mathrm { \dot { 0 } } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$and 1640–1550 cm<sup>21</sup> confirms the proposed mechanism, which is shown as follows.

elements.text: Thermal Stability of the Stabilizers as a Function ofTheir Stabilizing Efficiencies

Figure 3 shows the thermogravimetric analysis of the maleyl amide polymer stabilizers at a heating rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C / m m }$in air. The melamine amide polymer exhibits the highest thermal stability, since its decomposition starts at ${ \approx } 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and gradual degradation occurs up to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ;$then complete decomposition takes place up to $4 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$The thermal stability of the p-phenylenediamine polymer is lower than that of the melamine one, since the decomposition begins at ${ \approx } 1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$and after $2 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$the complete degradation occurs. The least thermally stable amide polymer is that of m-phenylenediamine, as shown in Fig. 3. These measurements were carried out to indicate the stabilizing efficiency of these compounds on the basis of their thermal stability.

elements.text: Effect of Maleyl Amide Polymers on the Discoloration of Photodegraded PVC

Here the effect of the concentration of the maleyl amide polymers on the degree of discoloration of photodegraded PVC is taken into consideration. Weight loss % of the photodegraded stabilized and nonstabilized PVC was determined thermogravimetrically. Also, the dielectric properties of photoirradiated samples were measured by using various concentrations of the stabilizers (0.5, 1, and 2% by weight) at different exposure time intervals (2, 4, $^ { 6 , }$8, and 10 h).

elements.caption: FIG. 4. Absorbance–time curves for rigid PVC photodegraded and stabilized by (a) 2%, (b) 1%, and (c) 0.5% by weight some maleyl amide polymers compared with dibutyltin maleate (DBTM) at $\lambda = 4 5 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$

elements.text: Results of the discoloration study are given in Fig. 4. It is found that the extent of discoloration decreases upon increasing the stabilizer concentration from 0.5% to 2% by weight. This change could be explained by the nature of the maleyl amide polymer structures and their ability to intervene with the conjugated systems via Diels-Alder addition reactions [18, 19] that disrupt the formation of conjugated double bonds, thus decreasing the degree of discoloration.
Electrical Properties

Weight loss measurements of nonstabilized and stabilized PVC using thermogravimetric analysis at a heating rate of 108C min<sup>21</sup> were carried out and are illustrated graphically in Fig. 5. This figure shows that the loss in weight of the PVC samples is lowest in the case of that stabilized by the melamine amide polymer, since the temperature at which the sample decomposition begins is $2 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and degradation then occurs gradually to reach 30% weight loss at $3 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$. In the case of nonstabilized PVC, the weight loss reaches 70%.

elements.text: PVC Before and After UV Irradiation. The values of the permittivity $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and the dielectric loss $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$for the investigated PVC before and after UV irradiation (for 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h) were studied over the frequency range from 100 Hz to 100 kHz at room temperature $( { \sim } 2 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$. The results obtained for $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$versus the frequency for pure PVC are shown in Fig. 6.

It is evident from this figure that there are differences in the values of $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$and $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$before and after UV irradiation (as a result of degradation [20]). The value of $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$decreases slightly with increasing frequency, a result which shows anomalous dispersion (similar behavior was noticed before in the literature [21, 22]). Also, $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$decreased after UV irradiation. This result can be explained by the decrease in the mobility of polar groups and, hence, an increase in the effect of the environment that facilitates the orientation of the mobile groups. In order to discuss the relaxation mechanisms associated with such dispersion, the $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$versus frequency $f$graph (see Fig. 6) should be considered. It is apparent that the values of $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$in the lower frequency range are higher. These higher values may be due to either DC conductivity [23–25] resulting from the increase of ion mobility or the Maxwell–Wagner effect or both. Also, the curves relating $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$and log $f$are broader than the Debye curve [26], thus indicating that more than one relaxation process is present. Fitting of the data was performed by a computer program. The best fitting was done by a superposition of two Fro¨hlich functions in addition to the conductivity term. elements.text: Stability of PVC in the Presence of the Maleyl Amide Polymers. In this investigation, the treatment of PVC with three kinds of maleyl amide polymers (melamine amide polymer, m-phenylenediamine amide polymer, and p-phenylenediamine amide polymer) using stabilizer concentrations of 0.5, 1, and 2% by weight was found to affect some electrical properties. The permittivity (e<sup>0</sup>) and dielectric loss $( \varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime } )$for the prepared samples over the frequency range from 100 Hz to 100 kHz at room temperature (228C), before and after UV irradiation for 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h, were studied. Examples of the dielectric spectra of PVC in the presence of the melamine amide polymer with different concentrations at room temperature, before and after UV irradiation for 6 h, are shown in Figs. 8 and 9. For all the investigated samples, $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$decreased slightly with increasing UV irradiation time in comparison with PVC, a result which indicates an improvement in the stabilization. Also, this trend seems to be affected by the type of maleyl amide polymer used and its concentration. This result is clearly detected when the percentage deviation of $\varepsilon ^ { \prime }$before and after UV irradiation is calculated for the different kinds and concentrations of the maleyl amide polymers at a fixed frequency of 10 kHz. The data given in Table 1 show that the melamine amide polymer gives more stability than the mphenylenediamine amide polymer, while the p-phenylenediamine amide polymer is in between.

The value of $\varepsilon ^ { \prime \prime }$in the lower-frequency region seems to be affected by the maleyl amide polymers. These dielectric spectra (Fig. 9) were fitted by a superposition of two Fro¨hlich functions in addition to the conductivity term. The width of the distribution of relaxation times P is around 4. The low-frequency losses may be due to the Maxwell–Wagner effect as a result of impurities such as catalyst, antioxidant, and others that are usually added to the polymers through the polymerization process [28]. The second absorption region value was found to be nearly the same as that for PVC. This result could confirm that this relaxation time may be attributed to intramolecular motion involving the rotation of various segments of the side group because the main chain motion is restricted [30].

On the whole, it seems that the results show that the type and the of the UV absorber play a role in the stability of PVC. To confirm that conclusion, the deviation percentages of DC conductivity r before and after UV irradiation were calculated and are given in Table 2. This table confirms that the melamine amide polymer gives more stability than the m-phenylenediamine polymer and that the p-phenylenediamine polymer has an intermediate effect. Moreover, this table reveals that the melamine amide polymer at a concentration of 2% by weight gives the best stability.

The greater efficiency of the melamine amide polymer stabilizer compared with that of the other polymers may be attributed to the presence of the free $- \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$group, which may have a role in the stabilization process. Wirth and Andreas [5] studied the effect of a b-aminocrotonic ester as an organic stabilizer for PVC. They noticed the stabilizing effect of this compound on PVC as its concentration increases. In spite of the expected negative effect of the amino group on the stability, the results indicated the stabilizing action of the b-aminocrotonic ester [5]. This finding may be attributed to the ability of the amino group to neutralize hydrogen chloride, as well as its ability to substitute labile chlorine atoms, as follows:

elements.text: CONCLUSION
• Addition of maleyl amide polymers achieves an improvement in the thermal stability as well as the photostability of PVC.
• The melamine amide polymer gives more stability to PVC than the m-phenylenediamine polymer, and the p-phenylenediamine polymer has an intermediate effect.
• The most favorable concentration of the melamine amide polymer is 2 wt%.

• The greater efficiency of the melamine amide polymer compared with those of the m-phenylenediamine polymer or the p-phenylenediamine polymer may be attributed to the presence of the free amino group $\left( \mathrm { - N H } _ { 2 } \right)$, which can participate in the stabilization process.
